## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sandhibhedajātaka* (Ja 349) is a narrative belonging to the *Catukkanipāta* (occurring in the *Cullakuṇālavagga*) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana in connection with the training rule against slander (*pesuññasikkhāpada*), occasioned by the unruly group of six monks (*chabbaggiyā*) who stirred up dissension through malicious gossip [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, a cunning jackal uses slander to divide two close friends—a lion and a bull—inciting them to fight until they kill each other, allowing the jackal to feast on their remains [Ānandajoti 2010; Winternitz 1933]. The Bodhisatta, then born as a king, reflects in verse on the tragic consequences of heeding divisive speech, and the Buddha concludes by identifying himself as that king [Ānandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883].
Scholars have highlighted this fable as a notable example of Indian wisdom literature shared across traditions; its central plot corresponds directly to the frame narrative of Book 1 of the Sanskrit *Tantrākhyāyikā* and the *Pañcatantra*, in which a jackal divides a lion and a bull [Mylius 2003; Winternitz 1933]. In terms of text reuse, DharmaNexus identifies exact matches (§1.1–4.4) between the text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, where the canonical verses are embedded within the prose commentary [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects minor cross-language alignments with the Tibetan translation of the *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthānasūtra* (D0287) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
